steps.body: Underneath both rules sits one principle: **the same whole shared among more people gives smaller shares.** 1/3 is a three-person split; 1/4 is a four-person split. The fourth guest's arrival shrinks everyone's slice — that's why 1/3 beats 1/4, even though 4 beats 3.

widget.prompt: Order these single pieces of the same bar from BIGGEST to smallest.

misorderFeedback.feedback: The reflex strikes — 8 sharers make far smaller pieces than 3. 1/3 outranks 1/8.
A six-way split can't beat a two-way split — 1/2 is the biggest single piece there is.

widget.missFeedback: Fewer sharers, bigger shares: rank by the bottoms, smallest bottom first.
widget.successFeedback: 1/2, 1/3, 1/6, 1/8 — the units climb DOWN as their bottoms climb up.

predict.reveal: Splitting among three leaves bigger shares than splitting among four — the smaller bottom number wins because fewer people are dividing the bar.

explanationVariants: Three-way sharing hands out bigger pieces than four-way — the same sandwich stretches thinner with each extra sharer.
Check the count: it takes only 3 thirds to rebuild the whole, but 4 fourths — so each third must be the bigger piece.

widget.prompt: Which is more of the same sandwich: 1/3 or 1/4?

options.feedback: Three sharers beat four — each third is the bigger bite.
The 4 counts SHARERS, not size. A four-way split spreads the same sandwich thinner: 1/4 < 1/3.

options.label: They're equal
options.feedback: Both are single pieces, but of different splits — the three-way piece is a third bigger than the four-way one.

options.label: You can't tell without measuring
options.feedback: Same sandwich makes it pure logic: more ways to split means smaller pieces, no ruler needed.

steps.body: The whole ladder at once: **1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > 1/5 > …** — unit fractions climb down as their bottoms climb up. Every new sharer at the table takes a bite out of everyone's share. The pie never grows; the forks multiply.

explanationVariants: Fourths of 12 cm are 12 ÷ 4 = 3 cm each — a full centimeter shorter than the 4 cm thirds. The finer split really is smaller.
Same ribbon, one more cut-line: the 12 cm now splits four ways, and 3 × 4 = 12 checks it.

widget.prompt: A 12 cm ribbon cut into THIRDS gives 4 cm pieces. Cut into FOURTHS instead, each piece is how many cm?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 cm is the THIRDS piece. Fourths split the same 12 cm one way further — each piece shrinks to 3 cm.
48 multiplied 12 × 4 — but cutting SHARES the ribbon: 12 shared among 4 pieces.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Share the 12 cm among 4 equal pieces.

widget.prompt: Watch one pie meet one extra fork.

panels.title: Three friends, one pie
panels.body: Three friends split a pie fairly — each plate holds a third. Generous slices all around.

panels.title: A fourth guest knocks
panels.body: The pie does NOT grow. The same pie must now split four ways instead of three.

panels.title: Everyone's slice shrinks
panels.body: Each plate now holds a fourth — smaller than the third it replaced. More sharers, smaller shares: 1/4 < 1/3, always and everywhere.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the doorbell's about to ring.
widget.successFeedback: The pie never grows; the forks multiply. That single fact powers every unit-fraction comparison.

explanationVariants: Nine sharers is the most crowded table here — each ninth is the thinnest slice of the three.
Rank by sharers: 2 < 5 < 9 people, so the pieces rank 1/2 > 1/5 > 1/9.

widget.prompt: Which is the SMALLEST piece of the same pie: 1/5, 1/9, or 1/2?

options.feedback: Nine ways is the most crowded split — the thinnest slice.
1/2 is the BIGGEST here — only two sharers. The question hunts for the most crowded table: nine.
Five sharers sit in the middle — nine-way splitting cuts thinner still.

options.label: They're all equal
options.feedback: All are single pieces, but of different splits — and the nine-way split spreads the pie thinnest.

hints: The rope stays 20 cm — only the sharer count changes.
Five kids now share what four were about to split.
explanationVariants: Five sharers now: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cm each — a centimeter less than the 5 cm each of four kids would have gotten. The latecomer shrank every share.
Check it: 4 cm × 5 kids = 20 cm, the whole rope accounted for.

widget.prompt: Four kids are about to share a 20 cm licorice rope equally — then a fifth kid joins BEFORE the cut. How many cm does each kid get now?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 cm is the four-kid share (20 ÷ 4) — but the fifth kid arrived before the cut. Five sharers now: 20 ÷ 5.
16 subtracted one share from the rope — but nobody has been served yet. The WHOLE 20 cm splits among the 5 kids.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count today's sharers (five), then share the 20 cm among them.

takeaways: Same whole + more sharers = smaller shares, every time.
Unit fractions climb down as bottoms climb up: 1/2 > 1/3 > 1/4 > …
When in doubt, make it concrete — centimeters don't argue.
steps.teaser: one final guard rule protects every comparison you've learned: the wholes must match.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **The pie never grows — the forks multiply.** Every extra sharer shrinks every slice. So a piece's size runs OPPOSITE to the bottom number: bigger bottom, more forks, smaller piece.

explanationVariants: Three forks beat six — each third is twice the size of a sixth.

widget.prompt: Same pie: which is the BIGGER piece, 1/6 or 1/3?

options.feedback: Three-way splitting leaves bigger slices than six-way.
Six forks at the table — each slice is thinner. The three-way slice is the big one.

options.label: Same size
options.feedback: Different splits of one pie can't match: doubling the sharers halves each share.
